UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                      )
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C                            )                 Docket No. ER26-3515-000
                                                      )



                         COMMENTS OF ADVANCED ENERGY UNITED

         Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”)

Rules of Practice and Procedures,1 Advanced Energy United2 (“United”) submits these

comments in response to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) revisions to the PJM Open

Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) and the Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load

Serving Entities (“RAA”) to establish the Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”).3 United

neither opposes nor supports PJM’s August 13, 2026, filing as a means to address the system

reliability issues as New Large Loads connect to the PJM system faster than new supply can be

brought online. United recognizes and agrees with the rationale behind IRAS: New large loads

that are contributing to the region’s resource adequacy shortfall, i.e., those that do not bring their

own new capacity, should be the first to face curtailment if and when load shed is needed.

However, IRAS as proposed leaves several important questions unresolved, particularly with

respect to how a New Large Load’s efforts to reduce its own footprint and secure its own

capacity are actually credited against its curtailment exposure, and whether IRAS’s central


1
  18 C.F.R. § 385.211
2

views expressed in these comments reflect the position of Advanced Energy United, but do not necessarily reflect
the views of any particular member with respect to any issue.
3
  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. “Proposal to Establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service and a Large Load
Registry to Address System Reliability” Docket No. ER26-3515-000 (filed August 13, 2026) (“Transmittal Letter”)
                                                                                                                    1
 incentive, to induce new large loads to avoid curtailment by bringing new capacity, can be

delivered at all given PJM’s own acknowledged lack of authority over retail-level curtailment

and compensation decisions. United’s comments below identify areas of uncertainty or concern

and offer specific clarifications and commitments PJM and the Commission should require

before this proposal takes effect.

I.     INTRODUCTION

       PJM is navigating a genuinely difficult situation, and IRAS reflects real effort to design a

workable response to New Large Loads connecting to the PJM system faster than new supply

can be brought online. United and its members have been active participants throughout the

Critical Issue Fast Path (“CIFP”) stakeholder process leading to both the RBP and IRAS filings,

and IRAS reflects meaningful refinement from the concepts PJM initially floated through that

process.

       However, the IRAS mechanism as proposed leaves important questions unresolved,

particularly with respect to how a New Large Load’s efforts to reduce its own footprint and

secure its own capacity are actually credited against its curtailment exposure, and how retail-

level cost allocation and compensation will be implemented consistent with the Commission’s

jurisdictional limits. United urges the Commission to direct PJM to act on these issues promptly,

both to ensure IRAS functions as the fair, incentive-aligned mechanism it is meant to be, and to

avoid creating a gap between wholesale design and retail-level outcomes.

       United does not oppose the concept of a curtailment and BYONC mechanism as a

necessary tool to manage an urgent reliability challenge, but United’s support for the specific

approach taken in IRAS is tempered by a fundamental issue: PJM’s proposal assumes a degree

of control over retail-level curtailment outcomes that PJM itself does not actually have. As

                                                                                                   2
 discussed further below, PJM can designate an aggregate megawatt figure for a zone or area, but

it is states and Electric Distributors, not PJM, who determine which specific loads are ultimately

curtailed. United urges the Commission to treat that jurisdictional reality as central to evaluating

IRAS, not as a detail to be resolved later at the retail level.

    II.      COMMENTS

          United respectfully identifies the following specific clarifications and commitments

needed to ensure IRAS achieves its intended purpose without creating unnecessary barriers to the

very loads and resources best positioned to help close PJM’s resource adequacy gap.


             A. Peak Shaving Adjustment Should Be Credited in the Eligible New Large
                Load Amount Formula
          The Large Load Registry tracks each load’s Peak Shaving Adjustment value, but the

Eligible New Large Load Amount formula that determines a load’s IRAS curtailment exposure

credits only BYONC and Allocated RBP UCAP MW.4 As a result, a load that has taken

concrete, state-sanctioned steps to reduce its own contribution to peak demand receives no

reduction in its IRAS curtailment exposure, the same practical result as a load that has done

nothing at all to address the shortfall it is helping to cause.

          Peak Shaving Adjustment is not a novel mechanism specific to this filing. It is an existing

tool under Tariff, Attachment DD-2, available to any end-use customer whose load reduction is

authorized under a state-codified program, and it predates IRAS entirely.5 PJM’s decision to add

Peak Shaving Adjustment as a tracked field in the Large Load Registry accordingly reflects

PJM’s own judgment that this value is relevant to a New Large Load’s profile and its capacity




4
  Proposed RAA, Attachment DD-4, § V(b) (PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3515-000, Aug. 13,
2026); Transmittal Letter at 37.
5
  Transmittal Letter at 65.
                                                                                                           3
 needs. Having made that judgment, PJM should complete the logical next step and ensure the

value it has chosen to track actually affects the calculation that matters most to the load: its

exposure to curtailment.

          This is the same gap United’s RBP comments identify with respect to the RBP peak-

shaving opt-out, and United’s RBP comments recommend the Commission direct PJM to amend

the Eligible New Large Load Amount formula in this proceeding.6 This docket is where that

recommendation must be resolved. United requests that the Commission direct PJM to revise the

Eligible New Large Load Amount calculation to expressly deduct verified Peak Shaving

Adjustment MW attributable to a New Large Load and comparable state-authorized reductions.

PJM should apply the deduction only to Peak Shaving Adjustment MW attributable to a New

Large Load and not already reflected in the load forecast as of the IRAS tariff filing date (August

13, 2026), or already reflected in the BYONC quantity, or another capacity adjustment.

          United does not propose that PJM independently determine whether a Peak Shaving

Adjustment or comparable demand reduction satisfies the requirements of the applicable state-

authorized program; consistent with the jurisdictional framework discussed further below, that

determination appropriately rests with the relevant state and Electric Distributor administering

the program. PJM should, however, retain its existing role in determining the MW value of a

qualifying Peak Shaving Adjustment. United therefore requests that PJM’s Tariff specify that the

deduction under this formula for a qualifying Peak Shaving Adjustment or comparable state-

authorized reduction shall equal the MW value calculated and verified by PJM pursuant to its

applicable procedures. This approach would avoid duplicative qualification review by PJM while




6
    Comments of Advanced Energy United, Docket No. ER26-3380-000, at 7 (filed Aug. 21, 2026).
                                                                                                   4
 ensuring that the amount of the deduction is based on the same PJM-determined and

performance-adjusted MW value used to reflect the program in the load forecast.


            B. Opportunities for DR/DER Aggregation as BYONC Should be Clarified and
               Expanded
                     i. PJM Should Clarify or Revise what counts as “New” DR/DER
                        BYONC
        Planned Demand Resource and Planned DER Capacity Aggregation Resources are

eligible as BYONC, an important recognition of demand-side value.7 These resources are among

the most affordable and fastest to deploy, making them well situated to meet the speed-to-power

imperative facing the PJM region. However, this eligibility is limited by the failure of the

BYONC framework to clarify what qualifies as “new” capacity for purposes of satisfying the

BYONC requirement. As proposed, DR/DER BYONC eligibility is limited to sites not registered

in or before the 2026/2027 Delivery year, or to incremental capacity tied to newly registered

generation or storage assets.8 This registration-based text excludes a site that has previously

participated, went dormant, and is now capable of providing the same incremental value. In

contrast, generation and storage can satisfy BYONC through Capacity Interconnection Rights

transferred from a deactivated resource or through repowering a generator that retired before

April 10, 2026.9 This provision is, appropriately, intended to allow new capacity from new

generation and storage assets at existing sites; this pathway to bring on new capacity at existing

sites has no demand-side counterpart. The treatment of future IRAS periods in PJM’s proposed

tariff revisions similarly lacks clarity. PJM has proposed a separate eligibility test for DR/DER




7
  Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, §§ VI(b)(ii)(1)-(2); Transmittal Letter at 54-55.
8
  Tariff Attachment DD-4, Revisions to the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff and Resource Adequacy
Agreement (Marked/Redline Format), Docket No. ER26-3515, at § VI(b)(ii)(1)-(2) (Aug. 13, 2026).
9
  Tariff Attachment DD-4, at § VI(b)(i).
                                                                                                       5
 BYONC once the system exits and later re-enters an IRAS posture,10 but this eligibility test

appears inconsistent; on plain reading the language precludes any site, new or reactivated, from

qualifying at all in a future IRAS period. PJM should clarify that DR/DER BYONC eligibility,

like generation BYONC eligibility, turns on incremental capacity value provided to the system

rather than solely on a site’s registration history, consistent with the incremental capability

standard discussed below.

        In summary, United requests that PJM create a clear mechanism for reactivated DR/DER

sites to be considered “new” for BYONC, comparable to reactivated generation, without

categorically excluding aggregations that participated before the 2026/2027 Delivery Year.

                      ii. PJM Should Clarify that Demand-Side DER can Substitute
                          Individual Sites or Customers

        United additionally requests affirmative clarification that demand-side BYONC should

have the option to substitute a departing site or customer for an equivalent new one.11 PJM

requires the Accredited UCAP value of a Demand Resource or DER Capacity Aggregation

Resource to “be demonstrated each year for a 10-year period” using the installed capacity the

resource had in its first Delivery Year.12 This requirement should not preclude a DER

Aggregator whose portfolio loses a site to ordinary customer turnover, relocation, sale, or non-

renewal from replacing that site and preserving its arrangement, such that its portfolio would

continue to reflect the same installed capacity it started with.

        The absence of a substitution mechanism would force a DER Aggregator to either hold a

shrinking, non-compliant portfolio as sites depart, or exit the arrangement altogether. This

consequence would fall with particular force on residential DER aggregators, since their


10
   Attachment DD-4, at § VI(b)(ii)(1)–(2).
11
   Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, § VIII(a)-(b); Transmittal Letter at 55-56.
12
   Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, § VIII(c); Transmittal Letter at 66-67.
                                                                                                   6
 portfolios consist of hundreds or thousands of individually enrolled households rather than a

handful of commercial or industrial facilities, and they experience predictable, ongoing customer

turnover as a structural feature of the business, not an edge case a one-off substitution request

could address.13 Aggregators are eminently capable of managing this turnover by bringing in

new customers if given a mechanism to do so.

           United therefore requests that PJM confirm that annual compliance will be measured at

the aggregation level, rather than requiring the same individual customer locations to remain

enrolled for ten years. Residential DER portfolios experience routine customer additions and

departures. That turnover does not reduce reliability when the aggregator maintains the required

aggregate capacity and performance. FERC should ensure PJM expressly permits a DER

Aggregator to add, remove, or substitute Component DERs during the commitment term without

losing BYONC status or jeopardizing its annual demonstration obligation. Substitutions should

remain subject to applicable registration, distribution-system review, measurement, and anti-

double-counting requirements. This clarification would preserve the ten-year capacity

commitment without converting it into an impractical ten-year commitment by each household.

                      iii. IRAS Must Accommodate DER Aggregations as Aggregations

           IRAS should expressly recognize DER Aggregation Resources participating under PJM’s

Commission-approved Order No. 2222 framework, consistent with the aggregation level

treatment requested above. PJM should provide a transition path for Planned DER Capacity

Aggregation Resources that begin under the IRAS framework and later enter PJM’s Order No.

2222 participation model. That transition should not terminate BYONC eligibility if the

aggregation maintains its committed capacity and satisfies the applicable market requirements.


13
     Comments of Advanced Energy United, Docket No. ER26-3380-000, at 20-21 (filed Aug. 21, 2026).
                                                                                                     7
                   iv. PJM Should Create Additional DR Products to Expand the Role of
                      DR in Addressing the Region’s Capacity Shortfall

       Some customers—including New Large Loads—may have the ability and willingness to

participate as DR if given additional options to do so, specifically limited duration DR products

that would carry more manageable curtailment risk given their particular customer profile.

Outside of this proceeding, United recommends that PJM separately develop additional DR

product options, calibrated to a capped number of event hours per year, that would expand

available DR in the PJM region, including allowing a New Large Load to self-provide a

meaningful share of its BYONC obligation through its own demonstrated ability to curtail or

shift load during those hours.

       A capped-hours structure of this kind would expand the types of customers willing and

able to participate as DR and would give New Large Loads a lower-cost, faster-to-implement

option for satisfying part of their BYONC obligation, particularly during the multi-year window

before new generation or storage can realistically come online, without requiring the load to

curtail an unlimited or unpredictable number of hours annually.

       This ask sits outside the instant proceeding but would meaningfully contribute to PJM’s

ability to address its resource adequacy shortfall, and would give New Large Loads another tool

to support that goal.

           C. IRAS Includes Important Elements That Should Be Maintained

       United supports several elements of IRAS that will promote fair outcomes and recognize

the standing value of demand-side and alternative capacity solutions and urges that these

elements be maintained in IRAS or any successor curtailment and Bring Your Own New

Capacity ("BYONC") framework.



                                                                                                    8
             First, BYONC's gating criteria explicitly recognizes incremental capacity created through

the utilization of Surplus Interconnection Service as qualifying new capacity,14 a more

permissive approach than PJM's own RBP proposal, which excludes SIS-based resources from

selling into the RBP. United’s comments in the RBP proceeding also identified several critical

barriers to full utilization of SIS that should be addressed separate from these two proceedings.15

            Second, PJM should likewise be commended for locking a BYONC arrangement's

Accredited UCAP value at whatever the resource clears in the RPM Auction for the first

Delivery Year of the arrangement, fixed for the full 10-year term, rather than subject to ongoing

re-accreditation.16 This is the right design choice, and stands in useful contrast to RBP, where

resources remain exposed to unhedgeable ELCC risk in revenue settlement for the life of the

term, an issue United's RBP comments raise directly.17

            Third, BYONC's inclusion of Planned Demand Resource and Planned DER Capacity

Aggregation Resources as eligible new capacity is likewise an important recognition of demand-

side value,18 though additional clarity and flexibility is needed, as discussed above. Likewise, the

Large Load Registry's tracking of Peak Shaving Adjustment values is a positive concept,19

though it is currently undermined by the Eligible New Large Load Amount formula, as discussed

above.


     III.      RETAIL COST ALLOCATION AND STATE COORDINATION
            As stated above, United supports the goal of IRAS: to incentivize new large loads to

bring their own new capacity, and to ensure that those that do not, and that thus contribute to the

 region’s resource adequacy shortfall, should be the first to face curtailment if and when load shed

is needed. But United is concerned that the entire incentive structure of IRAS rests on a premise

that PJM’s own filing does not itself deliver: that a New Large Load bringing sufficient BYONC

will actually be protected from curtailment. Eliminating or tightening the gap between PJM

implementation and state curtailment will be critical to success of IRAS. Specifically, PJM

designates only an aggregate megawatt figure for each Electric Distributor zone or area. This is

explicit in the filing, in which PJM says that it “will identify only aggregate MW values that

need to be reduced,” while “Electric Distributors, in coordination with the appropriate states

and/or RERRAs, LSEs, and LSE customers will determine which loads should ultimately reduce

subject to IRAS.”20 PJM does not direct curtailment of a specific retail customer. That authority

belongs to the states and the Electric Distributors that operate under state jurisdiction, consistent

with the FPA’s traditional divide between wholesale and retail regulation.

            This is not a peripheral detail, it is the lynchpin of whether IRAS functions as designed.

A New Large Load that invests in BYONC does so because PJM’s Eligible New Large Load

Amount formula promises that investment will reduce its exposure to curtailment. But PJM has

no mechanism to ensure that promise is honored once an actual Interim Resource Adequacy

Alert is called. Nothing in the proposed Tariff or RAA obligates an Electric Distributor, or the

state authority directing it, to actually exempt a load with sufficient BYONC from curtailment, or

to curtail non-BYONC load first, when the Electric Distributor makes its own retail-level

determination of which customers to reduce. But PJM has no mechanism, and by its own account

no authority, to ensure that promise is honored once an actual Interim Resource Adequacy Alert

is called. A load could do everything IRAS asks of it and still have no assurance that the entity


20
     Id at 26.
                                                                                                     10
 actually flipping the switch will honor that effort. The compensation side of IRAS has the

identical structure: PJM sets a wholesale rate and Electric Distributors implement it “in

conjunction with applicable state authorities and New Large Loads,”21 leaving open the same

question of whether the load that reduced its exposure through BYONC is the load that actually

receives the benefit of that effort, whether measured in reduced curtailment or in compensation

for load actually reduced.

         This same gap, wholesale design assuming an outcome only retail-level action can

actually deliver, is one that United’s RBP comments already raise with respect to cost allocation,

and United’s RBP comments state that this concern “applies with equal force to ensuring

consistency between RBP's cost-allocation and opt-out provisions and IRAS's curtailment

mechanics.”22 But unlike cost allocation, which the states are well positioned to address, and

which does not ultimately impact the outcomes of PJM’s implementation of RBP, here PJM is

delegating elements that are foundational to the function and impact of IRAS. This outcome

could have been avoided had PJM taken responsibility for curtailment of New Large Loads that

do not BYONC through adjustments to its own emergency procedures—while still allowing

flexibility for states to take additional action to more precisely target curtailment at the retail

level.

         If the Commission approves IRAS as currently structured, United recommends that PJM

commit to monitoring and reporting on the extent to which states and Electric Distributors have

adopted mechanisms, whether through the Virginia State Corporation Commission and Data

Center Coalition model-tariff process23 or comparable state-level efforts, that actually tie

 curtailment selection and compensation to BYONC status, so that there is no gap between the

treatment IRAS promises to a load that has committed to BYONC and the treatment that load

actually receives, simply because the latter falls outside the Commission’s direct jurisdiction.

Absent that assurance, IRAS risks functioning as an incentive PJM has designed but cannot

guarantee, with New Large Loads bearing the cost and effort of BYONC on the strength of a

protection no PJM-jurisdictional rule actually secures.


IV.    CONCLUSION

       United recognizes the unfortunate reality that curtailment of new large loads may be

necessary to ensure reliability for existing customers in PJM as demand rises faster than supply

and conceptually supports introduction of a mechanism to ensure that curtailment impacts those

customers contributing to the resource adequacy shortfall through their own failure to bring new

capacity to the system. The clarifications and commitments identified in these comments are

offered as opportunities to ensure IRAS achieves its intended purpose. United appreciates the

Commission’s consideration of these comments and looks forward to continuing to work with

PJM and other stakeholders as this proceeding moves forward.

       Respectfully submitted,
